instructions:
A PDF was filed by hand. Open the file at `attachments.pdf_path` and read it, then produce a structured summary.

Read it as a document, not as text: look at the figures, tables and plots. A result table usually settles what the paper actually achieved faster than the prose does, and a figure often carries the method. If the document is long, read the abstract, introduction, method and results sections in full and skim the rest.

`bibliography` must come from the document itself — its title page, header or footer. The filename is not evidence; it is whatever the person who saved the file happened to type.

`topics` is your judgement. These are the topics this archive tracks; list the slugs this paper genuinely belongs to, and leave the list empty rather than forcing a fit:
- reasoning-evaluation: Reasoning Evaluation — Benchmarks for reasoning and the methodology behind them: what each one actually tests, how contamination and memorization inflate a score, and where a reported gain fails to reproduce. The question the archive answers is which numbers a claim about reasoning can be built on.
- reasoning-faithfulness: Reasoning Faithfulness — The gap between a model's stated chain of thought and the computation that produced its answer: unfaithful or post-hoc rationalization, reasoning that is latent rather than written, encoded or steganographic traces, and what a monitor reading the trace can and cannot catch. The question the archive answers is when a visible reasoning trace is evidence about the model, and when it is only text.
- reasoning-training: Reasoning Training — How a language model acquires long-form reasoning: reinforcement learning against verifiable rewards, process versus outcome supervision, distillation of reasoning traces, and self-training. The question the archive answers is which training signal produces reasoning that generalizes, and what each one costs.
- test-time-scaling: Test-Time Scaling — What a model gains by thinking longer at inference: sampling and verification, search over reasoning steps, self-correction, and the length of the chain itself as a compute knob. The question the archive answers is how accuracy trades against tokens spent, and where that curve flattens.

`relevance` must have one entry per slug you listed in `topics`.

Rules:
- Write in en.
- Ground every statement in the supplied material. If something is not stated,
  leave the field empty rather than inferring it.
- No marketing language. Prefer the specific number over the adjective.
- Return one JSON object matching the schema exactly. No prose around it.

bibliography.abstract: string - the paper's own abstract, verbatim
bibliography.arxiv_id: string - arXiv id if printed on the document, else empty
authors: string - author name, in the order printed
bibliography.doi: string - DOI if printed on the document, else empty
bibliography.title: string - the paper's own title, exactly as printed
bibliography.venue: string - journal, conference or 'preprint'; empty if unclear
bibliography.year: integer - publication year, 0 if the document does not say

concepts: string - reusable ideas this paper relies on or introduces
datasets: string - datasets, benchmarks, corpora or simulators used
output_schema.limitations: string - stated limits plus any the reader should notice
output_schema.method: string - how it works, enough for a reader to explain it
methods: string - named methods, architectures or algorithms
output_schema.one_liner: string - what the paper does, in one sentence, no hype
output_schema.problem: string - the problem it addresses and why it is open

relevance.<topic-slug>: string - why this matters for that specific topic

output_schema.results: string - headline numbers, on which benchmarks, against what
topics: string - slug of a tracked topic this paper belongs to; omit any that do not genuinely apply

payload.title: Learning from Token Level Distributional Deviations for LLM Reasoning

bibliography.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has significantly advanced Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning; however, it faces a fundamental optimization instability: uniform token updates precipitate entropy collapse, leading to premature convergence to suboptimal strategies, whereas excessive Shannon Entropy maximization can cause entropy explosion, driving blind exploration toward incoherent reasoning chains. To resolve this dichotomy, we introduce the Independent Combinatorial Tokens (ICT) framework, which shifts the optimization focus from scalar uncertainty to the distributional properties of token logits. By leveraging the Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence between token logits distributions, ICT identifies tokens with distinctive distributional patterns as critical branching points for guiding effective exploration in LLM reasoning. Our theoretical analysis, grounded in both Shannon and second-order Renyi entropy, proves that selectively updating on these tokens regulates policy concentration: it reduces the overall distribution uncertainty measured by Shannon entropy, while controlling probability concentration captured by second-order Renyi entropy. This dual effect prevents over-concentrated token generation from weakening exploration and effectively stabilizes the training landscape. Empirical results demonstrate that updating only the top 10% of unique tokens on Qwen2.5 (0.5B/1.5B/7B) models yields an average pass@4 improvement of 4.58%, with a maximum gain of 14.9%, over GRPO, 20-Entropy, and STAPO baselines across seven benchmarks spanning math, commonsense, and Olympiad-level problems.
bibliography.title: Beyond Entropy: Learning from Token-Level Distributional Deviations for LLM Reasoning

contributions: A distributional criterion for token importance: a token's uniqueness is the Jensen-Shannon divergence between its logit distribution and the group-average distribution across rollouts, replacing scalar entropy with the shape of the distribution.

A theoretical account of entropy dynamics under sparse updates using second-order Renyi entropy and collision probability, deriving an entropy bifurcation — updating a token with probability above the policy's 'strategy purity' decreases entropy (collapse regime), below it increases entropy (explosion regime) — and positioning unique tokens at the boundary between the two.
The ICT framework and a Sparse-GRPO estimator that masks all but the top-k-percentile unique tokens and renormalizes the objective by the size of the active mask.

Evidence that unique tokens are drawn about equally from high- and low-entropy populations (ratio 1.03 on GSM8K, 0.99 on MATH), which is the concrete empirical break with entropy-threshold token selection.
result.limitations: The paper has no limitations section; the conclusion names only future extension to continuous domains. Numbers a reader should check before citing: the abstract claims an average pass@4 improvement of 4.58% with a maximum gain of 14.9%, while the contribution list gives 4.37%, 4.98% and 4.38% against the three baselines and Section 4.2 gives 3.38%, 4.31% and 3.94% per model size — three different framings that are not reconciled. Section 4.2 also states a 0.5B P@4 gain of +3.37% where Table 1's parenthetical for the same cell reads +4.37%, and the parenthetical deltas could not be reproduced from Table 1 by comparison against the base model, against GRPO, or against the mean of the three baselines, so what they are relative to is unclear. Beyond the arithmetic: models top out at 7B, and on the 0.5B and 1.5B models the AIME columns are at or near zero for every method, so the seven-benchmark average is carried by benchmarks where the intervention cannot move anything. Five random seeds are stated for the training recipe but no variance or interval is reported in the main table. Finally, uniqueness is defined relative to the sampled group, so the criterion depends on the group size G, which is not ablated.
result.method: For each generation step the group of G rollouts gives G logit distributions; their softmax average P_avg(.|t) defines what the group typically does at that position. A token's uniqueness score is u_{i,t} = JS(softmax(L_{i,t}) || P_avg(.|t)), bounded in [0, log 2], which measures how far this rollout's distribution deviates from the group consensus rather than how uncertain it is. A binary mask keeps tokens whose score is in the top k percentile, and the standard GRPO per-token objective (clipped ratio times advantage, minus a KL penalty to a reference policy) is applied only through that mask, with the normalization changed from the sequence length T to the number of active mask positions. A warm-up phase runs dense GRPO before sparse selection engages. The theory supporting this uses second-order Renyi entropy H_2 = -log C, with C the collision probability, and defines strategy purity beta(pi) = sum_a pi(a)^2. A first-order expansion gives the change in H_2 from nudging a token's logit as proportional to -pi(a*)(pi(a*)/beta(pi) - 1), so the sign flips at pi(a*) = beta(pi): updating dominant tokens collapses entropy, updating long-tail tokens inflates it. The paper's claim is that selecting distributionally unique tokens naturally lands on the boundary and so regulates concentration without optimizing any entropy term directly. Training uses VeRL with the GRPO recipe, averaged over 5 random seeds, with only the token-selection step differing from the GRPO baseline.
result.one_liner: Argues that Shannon entropy is the wrong criterion for picking which tokens to train on in RLVR, and selects tokens instead by the Jensen-Shannon divergence of their logit distribution from the group average, updating only the top 10% of these 'unique' tokens.
result.problem: RLVR applies gradient uniformly over all tokens, which drives entropy collapse and premature convergence; the obvious fix — training only on high-entropy tokens — pushes the other way into entropy explosion and blind exploration. Existing mitigations monitor or constrain entropy directly rather than addressing the cause. The paper's specific objection is that Shannon entropy is a scalar summary that cannot distinguish distributions with the same entropy but different shape, so two tokens with identical entropy can sit at completely different decision structures, making entropy an ambiguous signal for which tokens carry exploration-relevant information.

relevance.reasoning-training: A direct and testable disagreement with entropy-based token selection, which makes it the natural companion read to the high-entropy-minority-tokens line of work. The empirical crux is small and checkable: if the tokens that matter were the high-entropy ones, the set ICT selects would be skewed high-entropy, and it is not — it splits about evenly. That reframes the question this topic tracks from 'how uncertain is the model here' to 'how much does this rollout diverge from what the group does here', which is a claim about where exploration signal lives. The Renyi-entropy bifurcation argument also gives a principled reason why both dense updates and high-entropy-only updates fail, in terms of one quantity (collision probability) rather than two opposed heuristics. The caveat for this topic is scale: the strongest competing result in this literature is demonstrated at 32B, and this one stops at 7B.

result.results: On Qwen2.5 at 0.5B, 1.5B and 7B, trained on GSM8K and MATH and evaluated on seven benchmarks (Math500, GSM8K, MMLU-Stem, GPQA, AIME23, AIME24, AIME25), ICT reports the best average P@1, P@4 and Total at every scale. Average P@1/P@4/Total: 0.5B — base 5.65/14.48/10.07, GRPO 10.52/18.97/14.75, 20-Entropy 8.26/16.37/12.32, STAPO 9.54/18.29/13.92, ICT 10.95/21.75/16.35; 1.5B — base 16.41/31.80/24.11, GRPO 18.22/31.87/25.05, 20-Entropy 18.66/31.02/24.84, STAPO 19.89/31.52/25.71, ICT 21.93/36.53/29.23; 7B — base 37.78/55.25/46.52, GRPO 40.27/54.16/46.28, 20-Entropy 41.94/53.29/45.41, STAPO 41.55/55.52/48.54, ICT 42.99/58.37/50.68. Gains in P@4 exceed gains in P@1 at every scale, which the paper reads as evidence of more diverse correct trajectories rather than repeated ones. Training is on math only, but the improvement carries to GPQA, whereas the 20-Entropy baseline gains on math and loses on the non-math average. Sparsity ablation on Qwen2.5-1.5B/GSM8K: 10% unique gives P@1 66.23 and P@4 85.31, against 20% (63.37/83.31), 30% (64.45/83.76), the bottom 90% frequent tokens (60.62/85.08) and GRPO (57.45/78.45). Composition of the selected set: high-entropy to low-entropy ratio 1.03 on GSM8K and 0.99 on MATH.
